nameStory: The 'creeping snowberry' gets its name from its ground-hugging growth habit and the small white berries that look like tiny snowballs dotting the forest floor. The alternate name 'moxie-plum' connects to the famous New England soft drink Moxie, which was originally flavored with wintergreen - the same minty taste you'll find in this plant's leaves and berries!
description: Creeping snowberry is a tiny trailing vine that carpets the forest floor, staying close to the ground as it spreads. This delicate member of the heath family produces small white berries and has miniature evergreen leaves that smell distinctly of wintergreen when crushed. The entire plant rarely rises more than a few inches tall, instead spreading horizontally to form low mats in cool, shaded woods.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that trail and root as they go - never growing upright like its cousin eastern teaberry

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval evergreen leaves, usually less than half an inch long, that release a strong wintergreen scent when crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small white berries that look like miniature snowballs, appearing in late summer and tasting strongly of wintergreen mint

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems covered with tiny bristles that you can feel if you run your finger along them - these bristles give the plant its scientific name 'hispidula'

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white bell-shaped flowers that hang beneath the leaves in spring, so small they're easily overlooked but perfectly formed miniatures of heath family blooms

habitat: Look for creeping snowberry in cool, moist coniferous and mixed forests, especially under spruces, firs, and hemlocks where the soil stays consistently damp. It thrives in acidic, peaty soils and is often found in the same habitats as bunchberry and goldthread. This plant prefers the deep shade of mature forests and is particularly common in northern New England's mountain woods.

seasonality.spring: Tiny white bell flowers appear beneath the leaves in late spring, easy to miss unless you look closely at the ground-level mats.
seasonality.summer: Green berries develop through summer while the evergreen leaves maintain their wintergreen fragrance when crushed.
seasonality.fall: White berries ripen from August through September, standing out like tiny pearls against the dark forest floor.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist under snow cover, though the plant may be completely buried in areas with heavy snowfall.

funFact: The Mi'kmaq people of Newfoundland called this plant 'manna teaberry' and considered it such a precious find that discovering a patch was thought to be a gift from the spirits - quite fitting for something that tastes like natural chewing gum hiding on the forest floor!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its taller cousin eastern teaberry (wintergreen), but creeping snowberry stays flat on the ground while teaberry grows upright on short stems. Memory trick: 'creeping' stays close to the 'ground' - both words have similar sounds!
contextualKnowledge: Both creeping snowberry and eastern teaberry contain natural wintergreen compounds (methyl salicylate) that were once commercially harvested for flavoring. However, most wintergreen flavoring today is synthetic, making these wild plants a rare treat for those who find them.
compareHints: While eastern teaberry grows 3-6 inches tall with upright stems and larger leaves, creeping snowberry hugs the ground with much smaller leaves and a truly prostrate growth habit. Eastern teaberry also produces bright red berries instead of white ones, making them easy to distinguish when fruiting.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern teaberry is much larger and more robust than its relative creeping snowberry, with leaves 3-4 times bigger and bright red berries instead of white ones.
